subject: Banking
title: The Bank of Japan's Experiment
description: A quick, practical guide to The Bank of Japan's Experiment.

hook.text: Japan has fought deflation for 30 years. The Bank of Japan tried zero rates, negative rates, and QE.

buildup.text: Japan's bubble burst in 1990. Prices and wages stagnated for decades.

discovery.text: The BOJ pioneered QE in 2001, before any other central bank.

twist.text: The BOJ owns over 50% of Japanese government bonds. It effectively funds the government by buying its debt.

climax.text: Japan showed what happens when deflation takes hold. Central banks can create money but can't always create inflation.

punchline.text: 30 years of deflation. Japan proved money printing has limits.

quiz.question: What percentage of Japanese government bonds does the BOJ own?

details.summary: The Bank of Japan has pursued the most extreme monetary policy experiment in history, including decades of near-zero rates, massive QE, negative rates, and yield curve control, trying to escape a deflationary spiral since the 1990s.
details.whyItMatters: Japan is a cautionary tale of what happens when deflation takes hold. Three decades of extraordinary monetary policy have not fully succeeded, raising questions about whether central banks can always fix economic stagnation.
takeaways: Japan has maintained near-zero or negative rates since the late 1990s
The BOJ owns over half of all Japanese government bonds
Yield curve control was introduced in 2016 to target long-term rates

faq.question: Why has Japan been stuck in deflation for so long?
faq.answer: A massive asset bubble burst in 1989, followed by a banking crisis that destroyed consumer and business confidence. An aging and shrinking population further suppresses demand. These structural factors resist monetary policy solutions.

faq.question: What is yield curve control?
faq.answer: The BOJ sets a target for the 10-year government bond yield and buys or sells unlimited bonds to maintain it. This gives the central bank direct control over long-term borrowing costs rather than just the overnight rate.
